newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Rival Koreas claim Pyongyang's leading dissident.
newsitem.headline: Rival Koreas claim Pyongyang's leading dissident.

text.p: The fate of North Korea's top communist party theoretician hung in the balance on Friday after he spent a second night holed up in a South Korean embassy compound in Beijing where he is seeking asylum.
Seoul and Pyongyang made hectic efforts to claim Hwang Jang-yop, 73, credited with devising Pyongyang's quirky brand of socialism.
South Korean Foreign Minister Yoo Chong-ha and Chinese counterpart Qian Qichen held short talks on the crisis on Friday at a meeting of Asian and European leaders in Singapore.
Yoo told reporters the two men would meet again, but gave no details on how the talks progressed.
China has been dragged unwillingly into a heated row that has bred fears of renewed tension on the Korean peninsula and possibly a disastrous collapse of the North.
U.S. officials said the defection was another sign of strains in the Stalinist country that were also reflected in food shortages and reduced military training.
South Korean radio reported that North Korea would send a delegation to China to negotiate for the return of Hwang, who Pyongyang says was kidnapped.

In a report from Beijing, the radio quoted a Chinese official as saying the delegation would be led by an official at the level of vice-minister and include officials from the Worker's Party and foreign ministry.
China is torn between an old socialist comrade and new capitalist friend, but Western diplomats in Beijing believe it has little choice but to respect Hwang's desire to defect.
The stakes are high for Hwang, who holds the innermost secrets of North Korea's secretive government as an intimate of top leader Kim Jong-il.

According to the accounts of previous defectors, North Koreans caught fleeing the country can expect summary execution, or a lifetime in a North Korean gulag. Families of defectors, according to a pilot who defected last year, are condemned to "a life of slavery".
U.S. Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon said there was no indication of heightened military alert along the border between the two Koreas over the incident.
"I think it's another sign of strains in North Korea, a sign of possible strains afflicting the regime as well as the country as a whole," he told reporters.
"We already know that they are facing a hunger problem, a food shortage. We know that their training levels have been substantially below their norms for the military recently."
The State Department said it remained hopeful a joint briefing of North Korean diplomats by U.S. and South Korean officials on a proposed four-party conference on the Korean peninsula would go ahead.

The briefing, which was to have been held in New York, has already been postponed twice by Pyongyang because of its failure so far to conclude a deal with U.S. trader Cargill Inc. to import grain to relieve its famine.
In Geneva, U.N. and aid officials said North Korea, reeling from poor harvests after floods, will need foreign food supplies by April if starvation is to be averted.

The U.N. World Food Programme appealed on Wednesday for $41.5 million to stave off "a real possibility of famine". The Rome-based agency, seeking 100,000 tonnes of food, said people were receiving a quarter of their minimum daily food needs.
South Korean newspapers urged the government to use every diplomatic means to bring Hwang to Seoul.
"It is also important to use international public opinion and cooperation with the United States and Japanese governments," said a commentary in the Hankook Ilbo daily.

"It seems that Hwang will remain in the embassy compound for a long period as China is caught between South and North Korea and also worries about the effect the defection could have on China's dissidents," it said.
"But we don't expect China to send Hwang back to North Korea. Perhaps Hwang will be expatriated to a third country other than Seoul."
